families.name: Swarm intelligence
families.description: Population and colony methods driven by distributed social information, collective motion or shared pheromone memory.

families.name: Evolutionary methods
families.description: Population methods based on structured variation or combination, selection, reference-set learning and adaptive control.

families.name: Trajectory-based methods
families.description: Single-solution methods that explore a neighborhood trajectory through explicit acceptance and state-transition policies.

families.name: Hybrid / memetic methods
families.description: Compositions of population, trajectory, local-search, decoder and exact/heuristic subsolver mechanisms.

families.name: Constructive methods
families.description: Methods that build complete solutions progressively from domain-defined components, often followed by local improvement.

families.name: Other / music-inspired methods
families.description: Population-based or memory-driven metaheuristics whose scientific identity is not accurately represented as swarm, evolutionary, trajectory, constructive or hybrid.

algorithms.name: Particle Swarm Optimization
algorithms.time: O(ND) per iteration for the canonical graphless fast path; topology/social policies may add overhead
algorithms.applicability: Continuous bounded search spaces; generic platform infrastructure also supports alternative social/topology policies
algorithms.publication: Kennedy & Eberhart (1995), Particle Swarm Optimization, IEEE ICNN; Clerc & Kennedy (2002), The particle swarm — explosion, stability, and convergence in a multidimensional complex space, IEEE TEC 6(1), 58–73
algorithms.implementation: Flat particle-major buffers, deterministic target-owned RNG streams, graphless fully-connected canonical fast path, calibrated movement/evaluation parallelism.
algorithms.assumptions: The canonical implementation assumes a bounded continuous representation. Stability results depend on the chosen inertia/constriction and stochastic assumptions; topology changes the social guide but not the generic state model.
algorithms.convergence: No universal finite-time global convergence claim is made. Under the Clerc–Kennedy constriction analysis, stability conditions can be derived for the linearized stochastic dynamics; practical convergence still depends on objective, topology and parameterization.

algorithms.name: Artificial Bee Colony
algorithms.time: O(SD) per complete cycle plus objective-evaluation cost
algorithms.applicability: Bounded continuous derivative-free optimization with probabilistic recruitment and explicit source abandonment
algorithms.publication: Karaboga & Basturk (2007), A Powerful and Efficient Algorithm for Numerical Function Optimization: Artificial Bee Colony (ABC) Algorithm, Journal of Global Optimization 39(3), 459-471
algorithms.implementation: Canonical employed/onlooker/scout phases with one-coordinate perturbation, proportional onlooker selection, greedy replacement, abandonment counters and exact OptimizationContext evaluation accounting.
algorithms.assumptions: Finite bounded continuous domain; finite objective values; one-coordinate employed/onlooker perturbation and component-wise boundary clamping.
algorithms.convergence: No universal finite-time global convergence guarantee is asserted; ABC is stochastic and its exploration/exploitation balance depends on source count, abandonment limit and evaluation budget.

algorithms.name: Firefly Algorithm
algorithms.time: O(N^2 D) pairwise movement work per complete iteration plus up to O(N^2) objective evaluations
algorithms.applicability: Bounded continuous derivative-free multimodal optimization with distance-dependent attraction
algorithms.publication: Yang (2009), Firefly Algorithms for Multimodal Optimization, Stochastic Algorithms: Foundations and Applications, LNCS 5792, 169-178
algorithms.implementation: Sequential objective-sense-symmetric pairwise attraction with distance-decaying beta, additive uniform randomization, bounded repair and exact partial-sweep OptimizationContext accounting.
algorithms.assumptions: Finite bounded continuous box; finite objective values and pairwise squared distances; brightness ordering equals objective ordering under the configured optimization sense.
algorithms.convergence: No universal finite-time global convergence guarantee is asserted; practical behavior depends on beta0, gamma, alpha, population size, coordinate scaling and evaluation budget.

algorithms.name: Cross-Entropy Method - Continuous Optimization
algorithms.time: O(N D + N log N) per complete iteration plus objective-evaluation cost
algorithms.applicability: Bounded continuous derivative-free multi-extremal optimization using an adaptive diagonal normal sampling model
algorithms.publication: Kroese, Porotsky & Rubinstein (2006), The Cross-Entropy Method for Continuous Multi-Extremal Optimization, Methodology and Computing in Applied Probability 8(3), 383-407
algorithms.implementation: Independent normal sampling, elite maximum-likelihood coordinate statistics, fixed mean smoothing, dynamic standard-deviation smoothing and exact partial-iteration OptimizationContext accounting.
algorithms.assumptions: Finite bounded continuous box; finite objective values; independent-coordinate normal model; component-wise clamping is an explicit boundary policy.
algorithms.convergence: No universal finite-time global convergence guarantee is asserted; CE convergence requires additional stochastic/model assumptions and practical behavior depends on elite fraction, smoothing and evaluation budget.

algorithms.name: Differential Evolution
algorithms.time: O(ND) per generation for classical mutation/crossover, plus objective-evaluation cost
algorithms.applicability: Continuous bounded search spaces
algorithms.publication: Storn & Price (1997), Differential Evolution — A Simple and Efficient Heuristic for Global Optimization over Continuous Spaces, Journal of Global Optimization 11(4), 341–359
algorithms.implementation: Flat parent/trial buffers; classical mutation and crossover strategies; deterministic per-target RNG; calibrated variation and independent evaluation parallelism.
algorithms.assumptions: A population of distinct donor indices is required; the represented domain is continuous and bounded by the configured boundary policy.
algorithms.convergence: The implementation does not claim a general deterministic convergence rate. DE is stochastic; convergence analyses require additional assumptions on mutation, selection and persistent exploration.

algorithms.name: jDE — Self-Adaptive Differential Evolution
algorithms.time: O(ND) per generation plus objective-evaluation cost
algorithms.applicability: Continuous bounded search spaces; canonical DE/rand/1/bin self-adaptation
algorithms.publication: Brest et al. (2006), Self-Adapting Control Parameters in Differential Evolution: A Comparative Study on Numerical Benchmark Problems, IEEE TEC 10(6), 646–657
algorithms.implementation: Per-individual inherited F_i/CR_i proposals; trial parameters are committed only after strict successful selection.
algorithms.assumptions: Canonical DE/rand/1/bin donor feasibility and a continuous bounded decision vector.
algorithms.convergence: Self-adaptation changes the stochastic parameter process but does not introduce a universal finite-time convergence guarantee.

algorithms.name: JADE
algorithms.time: O(ND + N log N) per generation plus objective-evaluation cost
algorithms.space: O(ND) population plus O(ND) optional archive
algorithms.applicability: Continuous bounded search spaces
algorithms.publication: Zhang & Sanderson (2009), JADE: Adaptive Differential Evolution With Optional External Archive, IEEE TEC 13(5), 945–958
algorithms.implementation: current-to-pbest/1/bin, optional external archive, Cauchy F sampling, normal CR sampling and success-mean adaptation.
algorithms.assumptions: Continuous bounded domain; p-best ranking is defined from current objective values; archive ownership is explicit.
algorithms.convergence: JADE is an adaptive stochastic heuristic; no universal rate is asserted by the library.

algorithms.name: SHADE
algorithms.time: O(ND + N log N) per generation plus objective-evaluation cost
algorithms.applicability: Continuous bounded search spaces
algorithms.publication: Tanabe & Fukunaga (2013), Success-History Based Parameter Adaptation for Differential Evolution, IEEE CEC, 71–78
algorithms.implementation: Historical memories M_F/M_CR, random memory slot per target, improvement-weighted success learning and external archive.
algorithms.assumptions: Strict improvements define the success set; no-success generations leave historical memory unchanged.
algorithms.convergence: SHADE adapts sampling distributions from successful history but does not supply a universal deterministic convergence rate.

algorithms.name: L-SHADE
algorithms.time: O(N_kD + N_k log N_k) at generation k plus objective-evaluation cost
algorithms.applicability: Continuous bounded search spaces with an evaluation budget driving LPSR
algorithms.publication: Tanabe & Fukunaga (2014), Improving the Search Performance of SHADE Using Linear Population Size Reduction, IEEE CEC, 1658–1665
algorithms.implementation: SHADE 1.1 success-history semantics with linear population-size reduction, fixed physical capacity and shrinking active prefix.
algorithms.assumptions: An explicit evaluation budget defines the population-reduction schedule; the active population never falls below four.
algorithms.convergence: LPSR is a resource-allocation mechanism layered on SHADE; the implementation makes no universal finite-time convergence claim.

algorithms.name: Generational Genetic Algorithm
algorithms.time: O(N(C_S+C_X+C_M+C_f)) per generation without elitism sorting; O(N log N + N(C_S+C_X+C_M+C_f)) with elitism
algorithms.space: O(N * |solution|) for owned current/next populations plus representation-specific operator workspace
algorithms.applicability: Any complete-solution representation with compatible initialization, crossover, mutation and cloning
algorithms.publication: Eiben & Smith (2003), Genetic Algorithms, Introduction to Evolutionary Computing, 37-69; Whitley (1994), A genetic algorithm tutorial; Blickle & Thiele (1996), A Comparison of Selection Schemes used in Evolutionary Algorithms
algorithms.implementation: Generic fixed-size generational replacement with objective-sense symmetric tournament selection, representation-specific crossover/mutation, optional non-reevaluated elitism, strict solution ownership and common OptimizationContext lifecycle.
algorithms.update:
\begin{aligned}
P_0&=\{x_1,\ldots,x_N\},\\
(i,j)&\sim S(P_t;f),\\
(y_1,y_2)&\leftarrow X(x_i^t,x_j^t),\\
y_k&\leftarrow M(y_k),\quad k\in\{1,2\},\\
P_{t+1}&\leftarrow E_t\cup O_t,\quad |P_{t+1}|=N
\end{aligned}
algorithms.assumptions: The common evaluator receives complete candidates. Crossover and mutation semantics are representation-specific; the cloner must provide independent owned snapshots for mutable solutions.
algorithms.convergence: No universal finite-time global convergence guarantee is claimed. Asymptotic results require additional assumptions on mutation reachability, selection, replacement and elitism that depend on the configured representation and operators.

algorithms.name: Scatter Search
algorithms.time: O(P(C_f+C_I)+P b C_d+P log P) initialization; up to O(b^2(C_C+C_I+C_f+b C_d)) per simple pairwise round
algorithms.space: O(P + b) owned solution snapshots plus domain combination/improvement workspace
algorithms.applicability: Any complete-solution representation with domain diversification, distance and combination methods; improvement is optional
algorithms.publication: Marti, Laguna & Glover (2006), Principles of scatter search, European Journal of Operational Research 169(2), 359-372; Laguna & Marti (2003), Scatter Search: Methodology and Implementations in C
algorithms.implementation: Five-method generic Scatter Search template with quality/diversity RefSet construction, pairwise-new subset generation, strict distinct quality replacement and objective-sense symmetry.
algorithms.assumptions: The common evaluator receives complete feasible candidates. Distance and combination semantics are representation-specific; distance must be finite and non-negative.
algorithms.convergence: No universal global convergence guarantee is claimed. The strict RefSet replacement rule plus explicit stopping bounds ensures termination of the implemented run; global optimality requires additional exploration assumptions.

algorithms.name: Simulated Annealing
algorithms.time: O(C_move + C_eval) per attempted transition; O(C_delta) when an exact differential evaluator is available
algorithms.space: O(|solution| + |move| + |undo|); no mandatory per-transition solution clone on the reversible path
algorithms.applicability: Any solution representation admitting a stochastic neighborhood and reversible move operator; exact delta evaluation is optional
algorithms.publication: Metropolis et al. (1953), Journal of Chemical Physics 21(6), 1087–1092; Kirkpatrick, Gelatt & Vecchi (1983), Science 220(4598), 671–680
algorithms.implementation: Generic reversible trajectory engine, Metropolis acceptance, ten built-in scientific cooling laws plus custom schedules, allocation-free statistical-cooling fast path, exact-delta fast path and common OptimizationContext lifecycle.
algorithms.assumptions: The neighborhood must be sampleable and moves must be reversible for the zero-clone fast path. Cooling schedule assumptions depend on the chosen schedule.
algorithms.convergence: Classical asymptotic global-convergence theorems require sufficiently slow logarithmic cooling under irreducibility/communication assumptions. The practical geometric default does not claim that theorem.

algorithms.name: Tabu Search
algorithms.time: O(|N(x)| * C_delta + log M) per iteration with exact deltas; otherwise O(|N(x)| * (C_move + C_eval + C_undo) + log M)
algorithms.space: O(|solution| + M) for retained short-term tabu records
algorithms.applicability: Any finite enumerated neighborhood with reversible moves and domain-defined tabu attributes
algorithms.publication: Glover (1989), Tabu Search-Part I, ORSA Journal on Computing 1(3), 190-206; Glover (1990), Tabu Search-Part II, ORSA Journal on Computing 2(1), 4-32
algorithms.implementation: Allocation-free best-admissible neighborhood scan, attribute-based expiration memory, best-so-far aspiration, fixed or varying tenure, exact-delta fast path and reversible full-evaluation fallback.
algorithms.assumptions: Finite neighborhood enumeration, stable tabu-attribute equality/hash semantics, and exactness of any supplied delta evaluator. The attribute mapping defines which reversals or features are forbidden.
algorithms.convergence: No universal finite-time global-optimum guarantee is claimed. Classical behavior depends on neighborhood, attribute memory, tenure, aspiration and optional longer-term strategies.

algorithms.name: Reactive Tabu Search
algorithms.time: O(|N(x)| * C_delta + log M_s) per normal iteration with exact deltas; escape steps reservoir-scan N(x) and evaluate one selected move
algorithms.space: O(|solution| + M_s + M_f + M_r) for short-term, frequency and repetition memories
algorithms.applicability: Finite enumerated neighborhoods with reversible moves, domain-defined tabu attributes and a stable configuration signature
algorithms.publication: Battiti & Tecchiolli (1994), The Reactive Tabu Search, ORSA Journal on Computing 6(2), 126-140; Glover (1989, 1990)
algorithms.implementation: Explicit repetition detection, feedback tabu tenure, cycle-length moving average, reactive random-walk escape, optional frequency diversification, optional elite intensification, exact-delta fast path and common OptimizationContext lifecycle.
algorithms.assumptions: Finite neighborhood enumeration, stable tabu-attribute semantics, stable domain-owned configuration signatures, and exactness of any supplied delta evaluator.
algorithms.convergence: Reactive Tabu Search is an adaptive memory-based heuristic; no universal finite-time global-optimum guarantee is claimed.

algorithms.name: Local Search — Best Improvement
algorithms.time: O(|N(x)| C_delta) per descent step with exact deltas; reversible full evaluation otherwise
algorithms.applicability: Finite enumerated neighborhoods with reversible moves
algorithms.publication: Talbi (2009), Metaheuristics: From Design to Implementation
algorithms.implementation: Steepest-descent best-improvement scan with allocation-free neighborhood cursor, exact-delta fast path and reversible fallback.
algorithms.assumptions: Finite neighborhood; exact delta evaluator, when supplied, must match full objective evaluation.
algorithms.convergence: Terminates at a local optimum under finite neighborhoods and strict improvement, absent earlier generic stopping.

algorithms.name: Local Search — First Improvement
algorithms.time: O(q C_delta) per accepted move, where q is the number of candidates scanned until first improvement
algorithms.applicability: Finite ordered neighborhoods with reversible moves
algorithms.publication: Talbi (2009), Metaheuristics: From Design to Implementation
algorithms.implementation: First-descent scan that stops immediately at the first strict improving move.
algorithms.assumptions: Neighborhood enumeration order is meaningful; strict improvement prevents objective cycles.
algorithms.convergence: Terminates at an order-dependent local optimum for finite neighborhoods under strict improvement.

algorithms.name: Multi-Start Local Search
algorithms.time: O(S * (C_init + C_LS)) for S starts; C_LS depends on the composed local search
algorithms.applicability: Any representation with an initial-solution generator and a reusable compatible local-search procedure
algorithms.publication: Marti (2003), Multi-Start Methods, Handbook of Metaheuristics, pp. 355-368
algorithms.implementation: Sequential independent starts composed with the reusable v0.23 local-search procedure and one common OptimizationContext.
algorithms.assumptions: The generator returns valid starts and the composed local search respects the common procedure contract; probabilistic independence is not assumed unless supplied by the generator.
algorithms.convergence: No universal finite-start guarantee; under independent starts with fixed positive probability p of entering a globally optimal basin, failure probability is (1-p)^S and tends to zero.

algorithms.name: Iterated Local Search - Lourenco-Martin-Stutzle
algorithms.time: O(C_LS0 + sum_k(C_perturb,k + C_eval,k + C_LS,k))
algorithms.applicability: Representations admitting a reusable local search, owned cloning and a domain-defined perturbation
algorithms.publication: Lourenco, Martin & Stutzle (2003), Iterated Local Search, Handbook of Metaheuristics, pp. 320-353
algorithms.implementation: Canonical initial local search, perturbation, local search and acceptance framework; global best is independent from incumbent acceptance.
algorithms.assumptions: Perturbation produces evaluable candidates; cloning owns candidate state; useful basin transitions depend on the domain perturbation/local-search pair.
algorithms.convergence: No universal finite-time global convergence claim; asymptotic results require additional reachability or ergodicity and acceptance assumptions.

algorithms.name: Variable Neighborhood Descent
algorithms.time: O(sum_k C_LS,k) per non-improving sweep, with restart after every strict improvement
algorithms.applicability: Any representation with an ordered set of compatible reusable local-search neighborhoods
algorithms.publication: Mladenovic & Hansen (1997), Variable neighborhood search; Hansen & Mladenovic (2001), Variable neighborhood search: Principles and applications
algorithms.implementation: Reusable ordered VND over ILocalSearchProcedure<TSolution>; strict improvement resets to the first neighborhood.
algorithms.assumptions: All local-search procedures operate on one representation and objective; strict improvement is defined by the problem optimization sense.
algorithms.convergence: On finite spaces with strictly improving transitions, VND terminates at a solution locally optimal for every configured neighborhood unless externally stopped.

algorithms.name: Variable Neighborhood Search - Mladenovic-Hansen
algorithms.time: O(sum_k(C_shake,k + C_eval + C_LS)) per complete non-improving shaking sweep
algorithms.applicability: Any representation with ordered shaking neighborhoods and a compatible reusable local-search procedure
algorithms.publication: Mladenovic & Hansen (1997), Variable neighborhood search; Hansen & Mladenovic (2001), Variable neighborhood search: Principles and applications
algorithms.implementation: Canonical basic VNS with ordered shaking, local improvement, strict incumbent acceptance and restart at the first shaking neighborhood.
algorithms.assumptions: Each shaking operator and local search are valid for the same solution representation; useful basin reachability depends on the domain neighborhood system.
algorithms.convergence: No universal finite-time global convergence theorem is claimed; asymptotic reachability requires additional domain-specific stochastic assumptions.

algorithms.name: Guided Local Search - Voudouris-Tsang
algorithms.time: O(|N(x)|*(C_delta_f+C_delta_p)) per guided scan on the exact-delta fast path; reversible full evaluation and active-feature scans otherwise
algorithms.space: O(|solution| + P) for P distinct penalized features
algorithms.applicability: Reversible move neighborhoods plus domain-defined unique active features with finite non-negative feature costs
algorithms.publication: Tsang & Voudouris (1997), Fast local search and guided local search; Voudouris & Tsang (1999), Guided local search and its application to the traveling salesman problem
algorithms.implementation: Canonical augmented-objective GLS with feature-utility penalties, exact objective-delta and penalty-sum-delta fast paths, and original-objective best-so-far ownership.
algorithms.assumptions: Active features are unique per solution; feature costs are finite and non-negative; optional delta evaluators are exact.
algorithms.convergence: Each strict augmented-descent phase terminates on finite spaces for fixed penalties; the finite penalty-update cap guarantees library termination, without a universal global-optimum guarantee.

algorithms.name: Reduced Variable Neighborhood Search
algorithms.time: O(sum_k(C_shake,k + C_eval,k)) per complete non-improving shaking sweep
algorithms.applicability: Ordered shaking neighborhoods; useful when repeated local search is too expensive
algorithms.publication: Hansen & Mladenovic (2001); Hansen, Mladenovic, Todosijevic & Hanafi (2017)
algorithms.implementation: Canonical RVNS omitting the local-improvement phase while preserving VNS shaking and neighborhood change.
algorithms.assumptions: Ordered shaking neighborhoods generate valid candidates.
algorithms.convergence: Finite MaximumCycles guarantees termination; no universal global-optimum guarantee.

algorithms.name: General Variable Neighborhood Search
algorithms.time: O(sum_k(C_shake,k + C_eval,k + C_VND,k)) per complete non-improving shaking sweep
algorithms.applicability: Ordered shaking neighborhoods and compatible reusable VND local-search neighborhoods
algorithms.publication: Hansen & Mladenovic (2001); Hansen, Mladenovic, Todosijevic & Hanafi (2017)
algorithms.implementation: Canonical GVNS using the existing VariableNeighborhoodDescentProcedure as its improvement phase.
algorithms.assumptions: Shaking and all VND neighborhoods operate on the same solution representation.
algorithms.convergence: Finite VND safety caps and MaximumCycles guarantee termination.

algorithms.name: Skewed Variable Neighborhood Search - Hansen-Mladenovic
algorithms.time: O(sum_k(C_shake,k + C_eval,k + C_LS,k + C_distance,k)) per complete non-accepting sweep
algorithms.applicability: Shaking, reusable local search and a finite non-negative domain distance
algorithms.publication: Hansen & Mladenovic (2001), Variable neighborhood search: Principles and applications; Hansen et al. (2017)
algorithms.implementation: Canonical distance-skewed recentering with sense-consistent minimization/maximization handling and independent original-objective best-so-far.
algorithms.assumptions: Distance is finite and non-negative; local search and shaking return valid candidates.
algorithms.convergence: Finite MaximumCycles guarantees termination; skewed recentering has no universal global-optimum guarantee.

algorithms.name: GRASP - Feo-Resende
algorithms.time: O(2 * sum_t |C_t| * C_g + C_eval + C_LS) per outer iteration
algorithms.space: O(|solution| + construction cursor + local-search workspace); RCL overhead O(1)
algorithms.applicability: Constructive problems with domain-defined finite greedy scores, restartable candidate cursors and compatible local search
algorithms.publication: Feo & Resende (1989), A probabilistic heuristic for a computationally difficult set covering problem; Feo & Resende (1995), Greedy Randomized Adaptive Search Procedures
algorithms.implementation: Canonical adaptive threshold-RCL construction; two allocation-free candidate scans; uniform reservoir sampling; reusable local search; common OptimizationContext.
algorithms.update:
\begin{aligned}
c_{\min}&=\min_{e\in C}c(e),\qquad
c_{\max}=\max_{e\in C}c(e),\\
\tau_\alpha&=c_{\min}+\alpha(c_{\max}-c_{\min}),\\
RCL_\alpha&=\{e\in C:c(e)\le\tau_\alpha\},\\
x'&=LS(x)
\end{aligned}
algorithms.assumptions: The domain supplies a complete constructive model with finite side-effect-free greedy scores, restartable candidate cursors and a compatible local search.
algorithms.convergence: No unconditional finite-time global convergence claim; with positive probability of reaching a globally optimal basin and indefinitely many independent iterations, failure probability tends to zero.

algorithms.name: Reactive GRASP - Prais-Ribeiro
algorithms.time: Canonical GRASP construction/local-search cost plus O(m) alpha sampling and periodic O(m) probability updates
algorithms.space: Canonical GRASP workspace plus O(m) reactive alpha statistics
algorithms.applicability: Constructive problems with strictly positive objective values, reusable GRASP construction and compatible local search
algorithms.publication: Prais & Ribeiro (2000), Reactive GRASP: An Application to a Matrix Decomposition Problem in TDMA Traffic Assignment
algorithms.implementation: Per-run discrete alpha controller, uniform initial probabilities, online per-alpha means, periodic Prais-Ribeiro ratio updates, canonical GRASP construction and common lifecycle.
algorithms.assumptions: Configured alpha values are finite and unique in [0,1]; the canonical ratio update requires strictly positive objective observations.
algorithms.convergence: No unconditional finite-time global convergence claim; adaptive alpha probabilities preserve stochastic sampling while useful alpha values retain positive probability.

algorithms.name: GRASP with Path Relinking
algorithms.time: Canonical GRASP + online pairwise PR; optional EvPR adds O(E^2*C_PR) per evolutionary generation plus optional offspring local-search cost.
algorithms.space: O(E*|solution| + path workspace) online; EvPR keeps bounded current/next elite populations, still O(E*|solution|), plus O(P_k) pooled randomized-path probes.
algorithms.applicability: Finite attribute-based path spaces with GRASP construction, compatible local search, non-negative integral distance and target-directed reversible moves
algorithms.publication: Resende & Werneck (2004), A Hybrid Heuristic for the p-Median Problem; Aiex et al. (2005), GRASP with Path Relinking for Three-Index Assignment; Resende et al. (2010), GRASP and path relinking for the max-min diversity problem; Ribeiro & Resende (2012), Path-relinking intensification methods for stochastic local search algorithms.
algorithms.implementation: Canonical GRASP + reusable local search + quality/diversity elite memory + configurable advanced pairwise path relinking + optional Resende-Werneck generational Evolutionary Path Relinking.
algorithms.assumptions: Finite non-negative integral path distance; nonempty target-directed move set at positive distance; reversible moves; exact optional deltas; finite randomized-RCL objectives; EvPR starts from at least two elites.
algorithms.convergence: Strict integral-distance decrease gives finite pairwise path termination when uncapped; EvPR stops at the first non-improving generation best or its generation cap; no unconditional global-optimum guarantee is claimed.

algorithms.name: Threshold Accepting
algorithms.time: O(C_move + C_eval) per attempted transition; O(C_delta) when an exact move-objective evaluator is available
algorithms.space: O(|solution| + |move| + |undo|); O(1) acceptance state beyond the domain trajectory workspace
algorithms.applicability: Any solution representation admitting a stochastic neighborhood and reversible move operator; exact delta evaluation is optional
algorithms.publication: Dueck & Scheuer (1990), Threshold accepting: A general purpose optimization algorithm appearing superior to simulated annealing, Journal of Computational Physics 90(1), 161-175
algorithms.implementation: Deterministic sense-aware threshold acceptance over the generic reversible trajectory executor, exact-delta fast path, three built-in monotone threshold schedules and common OptimizationContext lifecycle.
algorithms.assumptions: Candidate objective values are finite; reversible moves and optional delta evaluations are exact; built-in threshold schedules are non-negative and non-increasing.
algorithms.convergence: Finite termination follows from an active finite generic stopping criterion, neighborhood exhaustion, or a schedule reaching the configured minimum when threshold stopping is enabled. No unconditional finite-time global-optimality guarantee is claimed.

algorithms.name: Great Deluge Algorithm
algorithms.time: O(C_move + C_eval) per attempted transition; O(C_delta) when an exact move-objective evaluator is available
algorithms.space: O(|solution| + |move| + |undo|); O(1) water-level state beyond the domain trajectory workspace
algorithms.applicability: Any solution representation admitting a stochastic neighborhood and reversible move operator; exact delta evaluation is optional
algorithms.publication: Dueck (1993), New Optimization Heuristics: The Great Deluge Algorithm and the Record-to-Record Travel, Journal of Computational Physics 104(1), 86-92
algorithms.implementation: Classical absolute water-level acceptance with initial level equal to the initial objective, one positive linear rain-speed parameter, exact-delta reversible execution and accepted-visit best accounting.
algorithms.assumptions: Candidate objectives and water levels are finite; rain speed is positive and expressed in objective units; reversible moves and optional exact candidate-objective evaluations are exact.
algorithms.convergence: No unconditional global-optimality guarantee is claimed. Positive linear rain speed progressively tightens the classical boundary; practical termination uses the common stopping contract.

algorithms.name: Record-to-Record Travel
algorithms.time: O(C_move + C_eval) per attempted transition; O(C_delta) when an exact move-objective evaluator is available
algorithms.space: O(|solution| + |move| + |undo|); O(1) record-deviation state beyond the domain trajectory workspace
algorithms.applicability: Any solution representation admitting a stochastic neighborhood and reversible move operator; exact delta evaluation is optional
algorithms.publication: Dueck (1993), New Optimization Heuristics: The Great Deluge Algorithm and the Record-to-Record Travel, Journal of Computational Physics 104(1), 86-92
algorithms.implementation: Classical fixed absolute deviation around the best accepted record, exact-delta reversible execution and probe-versus-visited best-so-far accounting.
algorithms.assumptions: Candidate and record objectives are finite; deviation is non-negative and expressed in objective units; record updates come only from accepted visited states.
algorithms.convergence: With positive fixed deviation RRT may continue inside the record band indefinitely. No universal finite-time global convergence claim is made; termination uses the common stopping contract.

algorithms.name: Late Acceptance Hill Climbing
algorithms.time: O(C_move + C_eval) per attempted transition; O(C_delta) with an exact move-objective evaluator
algorithms.space: O(|solution| + L) for a circular objective-history buffer of length L
algorithms.applicability: Stochastic reversible neighborhoods over any supported representation; exact candidate-objective deltas optional
algorithms.publication: Burke & Bykov (2017), The late acceptance Hill-Climbing heuristic, European Journal of Operational Research 258(1), 70-78
algorithms.implementation: Final Burke-Bykov history-reference acceptance, non-worsening hill-climbing safeguard, monotone-quality circular history, exact-delta fast path and visited-state best accounting.
algorithms.assumptions: History length is positive; candidate objective comparisons are finite; optional exact deltas agree with full evaluation; maximization mirrors the quality ordering.
algorithms.convergence: No universal finite-time global convergence claim is made. With L=1, acceptance reduces to non-worsening hill climbing; for L>1 the retained history improves monotonically in objective quality.

algorithms.name: Demon-Based Acceptance
algorithms.time: O(C_move + C_eval) per attempted transition; O(C_delta) with an exact move-objective evaluator
algorithms.space: O(|solution|) plus O(1) Demon credit state beyond domain move workspace
algorithms.applicability: Stochastic reversible neighborhoods over any supported representation; InitialCredit is an absolute objective-scale parameter
algorithms.publication: Talbi (2009), Single-Solution Based Metaheuristics, Metaheuristics: From Design to Implementation, Chapter 2; energy-exchange origin Creutz (1983)
algorithms.implementation: Deterministic conserved-credit Demon acceptance with O(1) state, exact-delta reversible fast path, sense symmetry and visited-state best accounting.
algorithms.assumptions: InitialCredit is finite and non-negative; objective values are finite; exact deltas agree with full evaluation; maximization mirrors the energy orientation.
algorithms.convergence: No universal finite-time global convergence claim is made. Accepted minimization moves preserve f(x)+D in exact arithmetic; rejected moves preserve both x and D.

algorithms.name: Iterated Greedy - Ruiz-Stützle
algorithms.time: O(C_D(d) + C_C(d) + C_eval + C_LS) per destroy-reconstruct cycle
algorithms.space: O(|solution| + |removed| + local-search workspace); O(1) core scalar state
algorithms.applicability: Component-decomposable combinatorial solutions with a valid destruction/reconstruction pair; local search optional
algorithms.publication: Ruiz & Stützle (2007), A simple and effective iterated greedy algorithm for the permutation flowshop scheduling problem, European Journal of Operational Research 177(3), 2033-2049; Stützle & Ruiz (2025), Iterated Greedy, Handbook of Heuristics
algorithms.implementation: Generic partial-destruction / complete-reconstruction cycle, optional reusable local improvement, strict or constant-temperature Metropolis acceptance, and independent best-so-far ownership.
algorithms.assumptions: Destruction operates on an owned clone; reconstruction restores a complete valid solution before evaluation; composed acceptance/local search respect the common lifecycle.
algorithms.convergence: No universal finite-time global convergence claim is made; strict acceptance is monotone but can trap, while stochastic destruction and Metropolis acceptance require additional irreducibility/recurrence assumptions for asymptotic global guarantees.

algorithms.name: Large Neighborhood Search - Shaw
algorithms.time: O(C_D(q)+C_R(q)+C_f+C_A) per complete destroy-repair-accept cycle
algorithms.applicability: Structured discrete or mixed problems admitting a meaningful partial destruction and complete repair pair
algorithms.publication: Shaw (1998), Using Constraint Programming and Local Search Methods to Solve Vehicle Routing Problems, CP98, LNCS 1520, 417-431; Pisinger & Ropke (2010), Large Neighborhood Search, Handbook of Metaheuristics
algorithms.implementation: Generic owned-clone destroy/repair trajectory with complete-candidate-only evaluation, strict-improvement default acceptance, pluggable acceptance and exact incomplete-cycle OptimizationContext accounting.
algorithms.assumptions: Destroy operates on an owned clone; repair restores a complete evaluable solution; objective values are finite; cloning preserves independent ownership.
algorithms.convergence: No universal finite-time global-optimum guarantee is claimed. Strict acceptance gives monotone accepted objective values on finite spaces; global reachability depends on domain destroy/repair coverage.

algorithms.name: Adaptive Large Neighborhood Search - Ropke-Pisinger
algorithms.time: O(D+R+C_D(q)+C_R(q)+C_f) per iteration plus O(D+R) at segment boundaries
algorithms.space: O(D+R+V) adaptive state plus cloned visited-solution snapshots
algorithms.applicability: Structured discrete or mixed optimization with multiple complementary destroy and repair heuristics
algorithms.publication: Ropke & Pisinger (2006), An Adaptive Large Neighborhood Search Heuristic for the Pickup and Delivery Problem with Time Windows, Transportation Science 40(4), 455-472
algorithms.implementation: Independent roulette-wheel destroy/repair selection, novelty-aware sigma rewards, segmented reaction-factor weight adaptation and geometric simulated-annealing acceptance.
algorithms.assumptions: Compatible destroy/repair removed-component representation; stable supplied solution equality for cloned snapshots; finite objective values; complete repair before evaluation; unique operator IDs.
algorithms.convergence: No universal finite-time global-optimum guarantee is claimed. Adaptive frequencies do not replace reachability assumptions on destroy/repair operators and acceptance.

algorithms.name: Memetic Algorithm - Moscato
algorithms.time: O(N(C_S+C_X+C_M+C_f)+sum_{x in C_t} C_LS(x)) per generation; ranked policies add O(N log N)
algorithms.space: O(N*|solution|) plus one owned local-search phenotype and local-search workspace
algorithms.applicability: Any complete-solution representation with compatible genetic initialization/selection/crossover/mutation, cloning and reusable local search
algorithms.publication: Moscato (1989), On Evolution, Search, Optimization, Genetic Algorithms and Martial Arts: Towards Memetic Algorithms; Krasnogor & Smith (2005), A Tutorial for Competent Memetic Algorithms: Model, Taxonomy, and Design Issues, IEEE TEC 9(5), 474-488
algorithms.implementation: Shared fixed-size generational GA engine with a generation-level memetic extension; reusable common-context local search; Lamarckian/Baldwinian learning; every-offspring, periodic, probabilistic, top-fraction and stagnation-adaptive application policies.
algorithms.assumptions: Finite population; compatible complete-solution genetic operators; owned cloning; local improvement never returns a solution worse than its starting objective; common stopping and evaluation accounting remain authoritative.
algorithms.convergence: No unconditional global-optimum guarantee is claimed. The implementation preserves the stochastic GA lifecycle while local-search pressure changes exploitation; finite evaluation/generation/cancellation limits still terminate execution.

algorithms.name: Ant System - Dorigo-Maniezzo-Colorni
algorithms.time: O(sum over ants and construction steps of feasible-candidate scans) per full iteration, plus objective-evaluation cost
algorithms.space: O(|P| + colony solution/key-path storage); lazy global evaporation is O(1)
algorithms.applicability: Finite constructive binary, integer, permutation, combinatorial and mixed discrete search spaces with typed feasibility, heuristic-information and pheromone-key contracts
algorithms.publication: Dorigo, Maniezzo & Colorni (1996), Ant System: Optimization by a Colony of Cooperating Agents, IEEE Transactions on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics, Part B 26(1), 29-41
algorithms.implementation: Generic proportional pheromone/heuristic construction with log-space Gumbel-max sampling, sparse lazy exact evaporation, all-ant global reinforcement, explicit deposit policies and common OptimizationContext accounting.
algorithms.assumptions: Finite constructive feasibility; strictly positive finite pheromone; strictly positive finite heuristic information when beta>0; finite non-negative domain-appropriate deposits.
algorithms.convergence: No universal finite-time global-convergence claim is made for generic Ant System. Later bounded or convergence-oriented ACO variants have distinct assumptions and identities.

algorithms.name: Ant Colony System - Dorigo-Gambardella
algorithms.time: O(sum over ants and construction steps of feasible-candidate scans) per iteration, plus objective-evaluation cost
algorithms.applicability: Finite constructive combinatorial search spaces with typed feasibility, heuristic information and pheromone keys
algorithms.publication: Dorigo & Gambardella (1997), Ant Colony System: A Cooperative Learning Approach to the Traveling Salesman Problem, IEEE Transactions on Evolutionary Computation 1(1), 53-66
algorithms.implementation: Generic ACS pseudo-random proportional transition, local pheromone update and best-so-far global reinforcement over the shared ACO construction engine.
algorithms.assumptions: Finite feasible candidate sets; strictly-positive pheromone; strictly-positive heuristic information when beta is positive.
algorithms.convergence: No universal finite-time global convergence claim is made; persistent stochastic construction remains when q0 is below one.

algorithms.name: MAX-MIN Ant System - Stutzle-Hoos
algorithms.time: O(sum over ants and construction steps of feasible-candidate scans) per iteration, plus objective-evaluation cost
algorithms.space: O(|P| + best path + construction workspace) with bounded sparse lazy pheromone memory
algorithms.applicability: Finite constructive combinatorial search spaces with typed feasibility, heuristic information and pheromone keys
algorithms.publication: Stutzle & Hoos (2000), MAX-MIN Ant System, Future Generation Computer Systems 16(8), 889-914
algorithms.implementation: Generic MMAS best-only reinforcement, pheromone bounds, configurable iteration-best/best-so-far source and optional stagnation restart.
algorithms.assumptions: Finite feasible construction; nonnegative finite deposit; initial pheromone inside the configured bounds.
algorithms.convergence: Pheromone bounds preserve positive sampling support; no universal finite-time global optimum guarantee is asserted.

algorithms.name: Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy
algorithms.time: O(lambda n^2 + n^3) per complete generation plus objective-evaluation cost
algorithms.applicability: Bounded continuous derivative-free optimization; especially non-separable and ill-conditioned objectives
algorithms.publication: Hansen & Ostermeier (2001), Completely Derandomized Self-Adaptation in Evolution Strategies, Evolutionary Computation 9(2), 159-195
algorithms.implementation: Canonical full-covariance CMA-ES with positive logarithmic recombination, evolution-path cumulation, cumulative step-size adaptation, rank-one/rank-mu covariance updates and dependency-free symmetric eigendecomposition.
algorithms.update: \begin{aligned}x_k&=m+\sigma BDz_k,\quad z_k\sim\mathcal N(0,I),\\m^+&=\sum_{i=1}^{\mu}w_i x_{i:\lambda},\\\sigma^+&=\sigma\exp\left(\frac{c_{\sigma}}{d_{\sigma}}\left(\frac{\lVert p_{\sigma}\rVert}{\chi_n}-1\right)\right),\\C^+&=(1-c_1-c_{\mu})C+c_1p_cp_c^{\mathsf T}+c_{\mu}\sum_{i=1}^{\mu}w_i y_i y_i^{\mathsf T}\end{aligned}
algorithms.assumptions: Finite bounded continuous domain; finite objective values; symmetric positive-definite covariance up to the numerical eigenvalue floor.
algorithms.convergence: No universal finite-time global convergence guarantee is asserted; behavior depends on objective structure, persistent stochastic sampling, adaptation parameters and boundary handling.

algorithms.name: Active CMA-ES
algorithms.time: O(lambda n^2 + n^3) per complete generation plus objective-evaluation cost
algorithms.applicability: Bounded continuous derivative-free optimization with full dependency learning and weighted negative covariance adaptation
algorithms.publication: Hansen & Ros (2010), Benchmarking a Weighted Negative Covariance Matrix Update on the BBOB-2010 Noiseless Testbed, GECCO Companion, 1673-1680
algorithms.implementation: Weighted active covariance adaptation with normalized negative unsuccessful directions, positive logarithmic parent recombination, CSA and positive-definite covariance reconstruction.
algorithms.assumptions: Finite bounded continuous domain; finite objective values; negative covariance mass is limited and covariance eigenvalues are floored before the next generation.
algorithms.convergence: No universal finite-time global convergence guarantee is asserted; active covariance adaptation remains stochastic and problem dependent.

algorithms.name: Separable CMA-ES
algorithms.time: O(lambda n) per complete generation plus objective-evaluation cost
algorithms.applicability: High-dimensional bounded continuous derivative-free optimization when coordinate-wise covariance is appropriate
algorithms.publication: Ros & Hansen (2008), A Simple Modification in CMA-ES Achieving Linear Time and Space Complexity, PPSN X, 296-305
algorithms.implementation: Diagonal covariance adaptation with accelerated Ros-Hansen learning rate, CSA and evolution paths.
algorithms.assumptions: Finite bounded continuous domain with a meaningful coordinate system; cross-coordinate covariance is intentionally not represented.
algorithms.convergence: No universal finite-time global convergence guarantee is asserted; the diagonal model trades rotational invariance for linear complexity.

algorithms.name: IPOP-CMA-ES
algorithms.time: Sum over restart runs of O(lambda_r n^2 + n^3) per complete generation plus objective-evaluation cost
algorithms.applicability: Multimodal bounded continuous derivative-free optimization with unknown useful population scale
algorithms.publication: Auger & Hansen (2005), A Restart CMA Evolution Strategy with Increasing Population Size, IEEE CEC, 1769-1776
algorithms.implementation: Geometrically increasing-population CMA-ES restarts under one common OptimizationContext and exact global evaluation lifecycle.
algorithms.assumptions: Finite bounded continuous domain; each restart initializes a valid CMA distribution and shares the global platform stopping contract.
algorithms.convergence: No universal finite-time global convergence guarantee is asserted; larger populations progressively alter the global-search scale.

algorithms.name: BIPOP-CMA-ES
algorithms.time: Sum over large/small restart runs of O(lambda n^2 + n^3) per complete generation plus objective-evaluation cost
algorithms.applicability: Multimodal bounded continuous derivative-free optimization combining large and repeated small population scales
algorithms.publication: Hansen (2009), Benchmarking a BI-Population CMA-ES on the BBOB-2009 Function Testbed, GECCO Companion, 2389-2396
algorithms.implementation: Evaluation-budget-balanced IPOP large-population and randomized small-population restart regimes under one global OptimizationContext.
algorithms.assumptions: Finite bounded continuous domain; large and small regimes share one global evaluation budget and best-so-far state.
algorithms.convergence: No universal finite-time global convergence guarantee is asserted; BIPOP diversifies restart scales through a two-regime portfolio.

algorithms.name: Harmony Search
algorithms.time: O(H*D) initialization; O(D+H) per improvisation plus one objective evaluation
algorithms.applicability: Bounded continuous derivative-free optimization using Harmony Memory consideration, pitch adjustment and worst-harmony replacement
algorithms.publication: Geem, Kim & Loganathan (2001), A New Heuristic Optimization Algorithm: Harmony Search, SIMULATION 76(2), 60-68
algorithms.implementation: Canonical fixed-parameter HMS/HMCR/PAR/absolute-bandwidth improvisation, component-wise bounded repair, strict worst-harmony replacement and exact OptimizationContext accounting.
algorithms.assumptions: Finite bounded continuous box; finite objective values; fixed HMS, HMCR, PAR and absolute bandwidth during one run; deterministic platform-owned random stream.
algorithms.convergence: No universal finite-time global convergence guarantee is asserted; behavior depends on Harmony Memory size, HMCR, PAR, absolute bandwidth, scaling and evaluation budget. IHS/GHS variants remain scientifically separate.

algorithms.name: Improved Harmony Search
algorithms.time: O(H*D) initialization; O(D+H) per improvisation plus O(1) PAR/bw scheduling and one objective evaluation
algorithms.applicability: Bounded continuous derivative-free optimization with fixed HMCR, linearly increasing PAR and exponentially decreasing positive bandwidth
algorithms.publication: Mahdavi, Fesanghary & Damangir (2007), An improved harmony search algorithm for solving optimization problems, Applied Mathematics and Computation 188(2), 1567-1579
algorithms.implementation: Canonical IHS parameter control with fixed HMCR, published linear PAR schedule, published exponential absolute-bandwidth schedule, HS improvisation and strict worst-harmony replacement.
algorithms.assumptions: Finite bounded continuous box; finite objective values; fixed HMS, HMCR and NI; 0<=PAR_min<=PAR_max<=1; 0<bw_min<=bw_max; bandwidth limits are problem-dependent absolute coordinate-unit parameters.
algorithms.convergence: No universal finite-time global convergence guarantee is asserted; IHS changes deterministic parameter control while retaining the stochastic HS memory/random/pitch and replacement process.

algorithms.name: Global-best Harmony Search
algorithms.time: O(H*D) initialization; O(D+H) per improvisation plus O(1) dynamic PAR and one objective evaluation
algorithms.applicability: Bounded continuous derivative-free optimization with fixed HMCR, dynamic PAR and bandwidth-free cross-coordinate global-best pitch adjustment
algorithms.publication: Omran & Mahdavi (2008), Global-best harmony search, Applied Mathematics and Computation 198(2), 643-656
algorithms.implementation: Canonical GHS dynamic PAR with no bandwidth parameter; pitch adjustment assigns x_i from a random coordinate x_k of the current best harmony, followed by explicit bounded-platform clamp and strict worst-harmony replacement.
algorithms.assumptions: Finite bounded continuous box; finite objective values; fixed HMS, HMCR, PAR bounds and NI; GHS has no bandwidth; K_i is a uniformly selected decision-variable index of the current best harmony. Final clamping is explicit platform repair for heterogeneous bounds.
algorithms.convergence: No universal finite-time global convergence guarantee is asserted; the global-best rule increases exploitation and can exhibit premature-convergence behavior without changing the published GHS identity.

algorithms.name: Self-Adaptive Global-best Harmony Search
algorithms.time: O(H*D) initialization; O(D+H) expected per improvisation plus periodic O(LP) successful-parameter averaging
algorithms.applicability: Bounded continuous derivative-free optimization with successful HMCR/PAR learning, bounded-normal sampling, piecewise bandwidth and corresponding-coordinate global-best pitch exploitation
algorithms.publication: Pan, Suganthan, Tasgetiren & Liang (2010), A self-adaptive global best harmony search algorithm for continuous optimization problems, Applied Mathematics and Computation 216(3), 830-848
algorithms.implementation: SGHS with HMCR~N(HMCRm,0.01) restricted to [0.9,1], PAR~N(PARm,0.05) restricted to [0,1], successful-value mean learning every LP, piecewise BW, and x_i^new=x_i^best pitch exploitation.
algorithms.assumptions: Finite bounded continuous box; finite objective values; fixed published normal standard deviations/ranges; successful HMCR/PAR values update their means every LP. BWmax=(UB-LB)/10 is represented coordinate-wise. Empty successful periods preserve prior means as explicit platform completion.
algorithms.convergence: No universal finite-time global convergence guarantee is asserted; SGHS changes parameter adaptation and exploitation/exploration balance while remaining stochastic.

algorithms.name: Novel Global Harmony Search
algorithms.time: O(H*D) initialization; O(H+D) per improvisation plus one objective evaluation
algorithms.applicability: Bounded continuous derivative-free optimization with reflected-best position updating, low-probability mutation and unconditional worst-harmony replacement
algorithms.publication: Zou, Gao, Wu, Li & Li (2010), A novel global harmony search algorithm for reliability problems, Computers & Industrial Engineering 58(2), 307-316
algorithms.implementation: Canonical NGHS: HMCR/PAR/BW absent; x_R=clip(2*x_best-x_worst); x_new=x_worst+U*(x_R-x_worst); uniform coordinate mutation with p_m; unconditional replacement of the worst Harmony Memory member.
algorithms.assumptions: Finite bounded continuous box and finite objective values; HMCR, PAR and BW are absent; mutation probability p_m is in [0,1]; reflected endpoints are truncated before interpolation.
algorithms.convergence: No universal finite-time global convergence guarantee is asserted. Canonical unconditional replacement permits deterioration and is intentionally preserved.

algorithms.name: Parameter-Setting-Free Harmony Search
algorithms.time: O(H*D) initialization; O(H*D) adaptive-rate recomputation plus O(H+D) improvisation and one objective evaluation
algorithms.applicability: Bounded continuous derivative-free optimization with OTM-derived variable-specific HMCR/PAR after rehearsal
algorithms.publication: Geem & Sim (2010), Parameter-setting-free harmony search algorithm, Applied Mathematics and Computation 217(8), 3881-3889
algorithms.implementation: Conventional PSF-HS random tuning + rehearsal HMCR=PAR=0.5 + OTM-coupled strict replacement + per-variable HMCR/PAR derived from Random/Memory/Pitch labels.
algorithms.assumptions: OTM moves in lock-step with strict Harmony Memory replacement; initial OTM is Random; rehearsal uses HMCR=PAR=0.5; pitch bandwidth remains problem dependent. If the PAR denominator is zero, HMCR=0 and platform PAR=0 is explicit defensive completion.
algorithms.convergence: No universal finite-time global convergence guarantee is asserted. Conventional PSF can drive variable-specific probabilities to 0 or 1 as OTM columns homogenize.

algorithms.name: Advanced Parameter-Setting-Free Harmony Search - Iteration Scheme
algorithms.time: O(H*D) initialization; O(H+D) per improvisation plus one objective evaluation
algorithms.applicability: Bounded continuous derivative-free optimization with iteration/dimension sigmoid HMCR and dimension-aware PAR
algorithms.publication: Jeong, Park, Geem & Sim (2020), Advanced Parameter-Setting-Free Harmony Search Algorithm, Applied Sciences 10(7), 2586
algorithms.implementation: Iteration APSF-HS only: published Equations (5),(6),(8); no OTM; fixed problem-scale bandwidth; object PSF excluded.
algorithms.assumptions: Positive NI and bounded finite continuous spans. D=1 uses the explicit right-hand dimensional limit HMCR=0.5. Object-dependent HMCR/bandwidth is excluded.
algorithms.convergence: No universal finite-time global convergence guarantee is asserted.

algorithms.name: Advanced Parameter-Setting-Free Harmony Search - Object Scheme
algorithms.time: O(H*D) initialization; O(H+D) per improvisation; Equation (9) at HMS block boundaries
algorithms.applicability: Bounded continuous minimization with a known target objective
algorithms.publication: Jeong, Park, Geem & Sim (2020), Advanced Parameter-Setting-Free Harmony Search Algorithm, Applied Sciences 10(7), 2586
algorithms.implementation: Object APSF-HS only: Equations (7),(8),(9); first-HMS rehearsal; strict replacement; minimization-only; target stop; coordinate-wise span lift.
algorithms.update: \begin{aligned}HMCR&=0.5+0.5\sigma(10-10(L_{mean}-L_{obj})/(L_{start}-L_{obj})-5/\ln D),\\ PAR&=HMCR\,\sigma(4/D-2),\\ b_i/(U-L)&=\Delta L_i/(L_{start}-L_{obj})\quad\text{or Eq.9 fallback}\end{aligned}
algorithms.assumptions: Known finite minimization target, positive finite coordinate spans, first-HMS fixed rehearsal, Loss_start greater than target while search continues.
algorithms.convergence: No universal finite-time global convergence guarantee is asserted.

algorithms.name: Differential Harmony Search
algorithms.time: O(H*D) memory plus variant-specific improvisation work
algorithms.applicability: Bounded continuous derivative-free minimization or maximization.
algorithms.publication: P. Chakraborty, G. G. Roy, S. Das, D. Jain, A. Abraham (2009), An Improved Harmony Search Algorithm with Differential Mutation Operator, Fundamenta Informaticae 95(4), 401-426
algorithms.implementation: Exact DHS structure: HS memory/random intermediate vector followed by DE/rand/1-style differential mutation with one F~U[0,1] and two distinct HM members; strict objective-sense replacement.
algorithms.update: \begin{aligned}y_i&\sim HM_i\ \text{with probability }HMCR\ \text{else }U(L_i,U_i),\\ z&=y+F(x_{r1}-x_{r2}),\quad F\sim U(0,1),\ r1\ne r2\end{aligned}
algorithms.assumptions: Bounded continuous search, at least two harmonies, finite objective values.
algorithms.convergence: No universal finite-time global convergence theorem is claimed in the paper.

algorithms.name: Exploratory Harmony Search
algorithms.time: O(H*D) memory plus variant-specific improvisation work
algorithms.applicability: Bounded continuous derivative-free global numerical optimization.
algorithms.publication: S. Das, A. Mukhopadhyay, A. Roy, A. Abraham, B. K. Panigrahi (2011), Exploratory Power of the Harmony Search Algorithm: Analysis and Improvements for Global Numerical Optimization, IEEE Transactions on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics, Part B 41(1), 89-106
algorithms.implementation: EHS keeps canonical HS memory consideration/random selection and sets per-coordinate fine-tuning width FW_i=k*sqrt(Var(HM_i)), recomputed from the current Harmony Memory.
algorithms.assumptions: Bounded continuous search, finite HM coordinate variance and finite objective values.
algorithms.convergence: The paper analyzes population variance and exploratory power; no universal finite-time global convergence theorem is asserted.

algorithms.name: Improved Harmony Search Based on Differential Mutation Operator
algorithms.time: O(H*D) memory plus variant-specific improvisation work
algorithms.applicability: Bounded continuous derivative-free minimization.
algorithms.publication: L. Yong, S. Liu, J. Zhang, Q. Feng (2012), Theoretical and Empirical Analyses of an Improved Harmony Search Algorithm Based on Differential Mutation Operator, Journal of Applied Mathematics 2012, Article 147950
algorithms.implementation: IHSDE memory branch chooses j,r1,r2 distinct and generates x'_i=x^j_i+F(x^r1_i-x^r2_i), F~U[0.6,1]; random branch remains uniform over bounds.
algorithms.assumptions: Bounded continuous minimization, HMS>=3, finite objective values.
algorithms.convergence: The paper derives population mean/variance behavior and reports empirical convergence; no universal finite-time global convergence theorem is claimed.

algorithms.name: Novel Self-Adaptive Harmony Search
algorithms.time: O(H*D) memory plus variant-specific improvisation work
algorithms.applicability: Bounded continuous derivative-free minimization.
algorithms.publication: K. Luo (2013), A Novel Self-Adaptive Harmony Search Algorithm, Journal of Applied Mathematics 2013, Article 653749
algorithms.implementation: NSHS dimension-derived HMCR, no PAR, fitness-standard-deviation threshold 0.0001, best-to-worst narrow randomization under low diversity and the paper's two perturbation branches.
algorithms.assumptions: Bounded continuous minimization, finite objectives and positive dimensionality.
algorithms.convergence: The paper motivates self-adaptation through diversity/intensity balance; no universal finite-time global convergence theorem is asserted.

algorithms.name: Adaptive Harmony Search with Differential Evolution
algorithms.time: O(H*D) memory plus variant-specific improvisation work
algorithms.applicability: Bounded continuous derivative-free minimization.
algorithms.publication: X. Zhao, R. Li, J. Hao, Z. Liu, J. Yuan (2020), A New Differential Mutation Based Adaptive Harmony Search Algorithm for Global Optimization, Applied Sciences 10(8), 2916
algorithms.implementation: Exact paper-defined aHSDE mechanism bundle: DE/best/2 pitch adjustment, Gaussian PAR/F sampling around learned means, successful-parameter weighted Lehmer updates, and linear HMS reduction against NFE.
algorithms.assumptions: Bounded continuous minimization, active HMS>=5, finite objectives and finite positive NFE budget.
algorithms.convergence: The paper evaluates cooperation of its adaptive mechanisms empirically; no universal finite-time global convergence theorem is asserted.

algorithms.name: Biogeography-Based Optimization
algorithms.time: O(N log N + N^2 D) per generation plus objective-evaluation cost
algorithms.applicability: Bounded continuous derivative-free optimization using rank-based immigration, emigration, mutation and elitism
algorithms.publication: Simon (2008), Biogeography-Based Optimization, IEEE Transactions on Evolutionary Computation 12(6), 702-713
algorithms.implementation: Canonical rank-derived species counts, linear immigration/emigration curves, equilibrium species-probability mutation, explicit elitism and bounded SIV repair.
algorithms.assumptions: Finite bounded continuous box; finite objective values; habitat quality ranking maps monotonically to species count; migration and mutation use the paper's linear rates.
algorithms.convergence: No universal finite-time global convergence guarantee is asserted; the implementation reproduces the stochastic migration/mutation mechanism and preserves elites explicitly.

algorithms.name: Cuckoo Search via Levy Flights
algorithms.time: O(D + N log N + p_a N D) per published generation plus objective-evaluation cost
algorithms.applicability: Bounded continuous derivative-free optimization with Levy-flight exploration and nest abandonment
algorithms.publication: Yang & Deb (2009), Cuckoo Search via Levy Flights, NaBIC 2009, 210-214
algorithms.implementation: Published Yang-Deb pseudocode: one randomly chosen cuckoo Levy-flight proposal, random host-nest comparison, replacement of a p_a fraction of worst nests by new random nests, elitist retention and ranking. The Levy-flight operator is realized internally with Mantegna's symmetric beta=1.5 construction; beta is intentionally not exposed as a configurable public parameter for this canonical identity.
algorithms.assumptions: Finite bounded continuous box; finite objective values; Levy steps use a fixed internal Mantegna beta=1.5 realization; abandoned nests are resampled from the search space.
algorithms.convergence: No universal finite-time convergence guarantee is claimed; global exploration follows the heavy-tailed Levy-flight mechanism and random abandonment.

algorithms.name: Bat Algorithm
algorithms.time: O(ND) per generation plus N objective evaluations
algorithms.applicability: Bounded continuous derivative-free optimization with frequency-tuned motion, pulse-rate local search and loudness acceptance
algorithms.publication: Yang (2010), A New Metaheuristic Bat-Inspired Algorithm, NICSO 2010, 65-74
algorithms.implementation: Canonical frequency/velocity/position update, best-centered local random walk, loudness-gated greedy acceptance, geometric loudness decay and asymptotic pulse-rate growth.
algorithms.assumptions: Finite bounded continuous box and finite objective values; loudness is positive, pulse rate lies in [0,1], and alpha/gamma are positive control parameters.
algorithms.convergence: No universal finite-time global convergence guarantee is asserted; the implementation follows Yang's published coupled loudness/pulse adaptation.

algorithms.name: Flower Pollination Algorithm
algorithms.time: O(ND) per generation plus N objective evaluations
algorithms.applicability: Bounded continuous derivative-free optimization mixing global Levy pollination and local flower constancy
algorithms.publication: Yang (2012), Flower Pollination Algorithm for Global Optimization, UCNC 2012, LNCS 7445, 240-249
algorithms.implementation: Canonical switch-controlled global Levy pollination toward the current best and local random flower-pair pollination with greedy replacement. The Levy-flight operator uses a fixed internal Mantegna beta=1.5 numerical realization rather than exposing a later variant parameter.
algorithms.assumptions: Finite bounded continuous box; finite objective values; global pollination uses a dimension-wise Levy vector and local pollination samples two distinct population members.
algorithms.convergence: No universal finite-time global convergence guarantee is asserted; stochastic exploration/exploitation is governed by the switch probability and Levy-flight scaling.

algorithms.name: Grey Wolf Optimizer
algorithms.time: O(ND + N log N) per generation plus N objective evaluations
algorithms.applicability: Bounded continuous derivative-free optimization using alpha/beta/delta leadership and encircling dynamics
algorithms.publication: Mirjalili, Mirjalili & Lewis (2014), Grey Wolf Optimizer, Advances in Engineering Software 69, 46-61
algorithms.implementation: Canonical alpha-beta-delta leadership, three independent A/C encircling vectors, arithmetic mean position update and linear a decrease from 2 to 0.
algorithms.assumptions: Finite bounded continuous box and finite objective values; at least three wolves; alpha, beta and delta are the three best current solutions under the configured objective sense.
algorithms.convergence: No universal finite-time global convergence guarantee is asserted; the linearly decreasing coefficient a moves the canonical model from exploration toward exploitation.

algorithms.name: Moth-Flame Optimization
algorithms.time: O(ND + N log N) per generation plus N objective evaluations
algorithms.applicability: Bounded continuous derivative-free optimization with logarithmic moth-to-flame spirals and a linearly decreasing flame count
algorithms.publication: Mirjalili (2015), Moth-flame optimization algorithm: A novel nature-inspired heuristic paradigm, Knowledge-Based Systems 89, 228-249
algorithms.implementation: Canonical moth/flame dual population, historical flame elitism, logarithmic spiral update, and linearly decreasing flame count from Mirjalili (2015).
algorithms.assumptions: Finite bounded continuous box and finite objective values; at least two moths; flames are the best historical positions under the configured objective sense.
algorithms.convergence: No universal finite-time global convergence guarantee is asserted; the decreasing number of flames and shrinking lower bound of the spiral parameter progressively emphasize exploitation.

algorithms.name: Whale Optimization Algorithm
algorithms.time: O(ND) per generation plus N objective evaluations
algorithms.applicability: Bounded continuous derivative-free optimization with encircling, random-prey exploration and logarithmic bubble-net spirals
algorithms.publication: Mirjalili & Lewis (2016), The Whale Optimization Algorithm, Advances in Engineering Software 95, 51-67
algorithms.implementation: Canonical WOA with scalar A/C coefficients per whale, random-prey exploration for |A|>=1, best-prey encircling for |A|<1, and the 50/50 logarithmic spiral mechanism.
algorithms.assumptions: Finite bounded continuous box and finite objective values; at least two whales; the best-so-far whale is the prey estimate and random-prey exploration samples the current population.
algorithms.convergence: No universal finite-time global convergence guarantee is asserted; the linear decrease of a from 2 toward 0 reduces the probability of |A|>=1 exploration.

algorithms.name: Sine Cosine Algorithm
algorithms.time: O(ND) per generation plus N objective evaluations
algorithms.applicability: Bounded continuous derivative-free optimization with sine/cosine oscillation around the best destination
algorithms.publication: Mirjalili (2016), SCA: A Sine Cosine Algorithm for solving optimization problems, Knowledge-Based Systems 96, 120-133
algorithms.implementation: Canonical SCA with linearly decreasing r1, r2 in [0,2pi), r3 in [0,2), and an equiprobable sine/cosine switch r4.
algorithms.assumptions: Finite bounded continuous box and finite objective values; at least two search agents; the destination is the best-so-far candidate under the configured objective sense.
algorithms.convergence: No universal finite-time global convergence guarantee is asserted; r1 decreases linearly from the canonical amplitude a=2 toward zero.

algorithms.name: Salp Swarm Algorithm
algorithms.time: O(ND) per generation plus N objective evaluations
algorithms.applicability: Bounded continuous derivative-free optimization with food-directed leaders and chain-following salps
algorithms.publication: Mirjalili, Gandomi, Mirjalili, Saremi, Faris & Mirjalili (2017), Salp Swarm Algorithm: A bio-inspired optimizer for engineering design problems, Advances in Engineering Software 114, 163-191
algorithms.implementation: Canonical single-objective SSA with c1=2 exp(-(4t/T)^2), leader coordinates sampled around the food source, and followers updated by the published half-sum chain rule.
algorithms.assumptions: Finite bounded continuous box and finite objective values; at least four salps; the food source is the best-so-far solution and the first half of the chain acts as leaders.
algorithms.convergence: No universal finite-time global convergence guarantee is asserted; c1 decreases rapidly toward zero, progressively contracting leader motion around the food source.

algorithms.name: Harris Hawks Optimization
algorithms.time: O(ND) population motion plus up to 2N rapid-dive candidate evaluations per generation
algorithms.applicability: Bounded continuous derivative-free optimization using surprise-pounce exploration, besiege modes and Levy rapid dives
algorithms.publication: Heidari, Mirjalili, Faris, Aljarah, Mafarja & Chen (2019), Harris hawks optimization: Algorithm and applications, Future Generation Computer Systems 97, 849-872
algorithms.implementation: Canonical HHO exploration plus four exploitation modes governed by escaping energy and prey escape probability, including beta=1.5 Levy rapid dives.
algorithms.update: \begin{aligned}E_t&=2E_0\left(1-\frac{t}{T}\right),\quad E_0\sim\mathcal U[-1,1],\quad J=2(1-r_5),\\X^{t+1}&=X_{\rm rabbit}-E_t\left|X_{\rm rabbit}-X^t\right|\quad(r\ge\tfrac12,|E_t|<\tfrac12),\\X^{t+1}&=(X_{\rm rabbit}-X^t)-E_t\left|JX_{\rm rabbit}-X^t\right|\quad(r\ge\tfrac12,|E_t|\ge\tfrac12),\\Y&=X_{\rm rabbit}-E_t\left|JX_{\rm rabbit}-Z\right|,\quad Z\in\{X^t,X_{\rm mean}^t\},\\X_2&=Y+R\odot L_{1.5}\end{aligned}
algorithms.assumptions: Finite bounded continuous box and finite objective values; at least two hawks; the rabbit is the best-so-far solution and Levy rapid dives use the beta=1.5 Mantegna realization.
algorithms.convergence: No universal finite-time global convergence guarantee is asserted; escaping energy E transitions the canonical mechanism from exploration to the four exploitation strategies.

algorithms.name: Big Bang-Big Crunch
algorithms.time: O(ND) per iteration plus N objective evaluations
algorithms.applicability: Bounded continuous derivative-free optimization using alternating random expansion and a shrinking Big-Crunch representative
algorithms.publication: Erol & Eksin (2006), A new optimization method: Big Bang-Big Crunch, Advances in Engineering Software 37(2), 106-111
algorithms.implementation: Published BB-BC minimal-cost representative option with Gaussian Big-Bang sampling whose radius decreases as alpha/t; no later local-search hybrid is mixed in.
algorithms.assumptions: Finite bounded continuous box, finite objective values and at least two candidates. The original paper explicitly allows the Big-Crunch representative to be either the center of mass or the minimal-cost candidate; this identity uses the published minimal-cost option so it remains well-defined for zero and signed objectives.
algorithms.convergence: No universal finite-time global convergence guarantee is asserted; the published Gaussian radius contracts proportionally to 1/t around the current minimal-cost representative.

algorithms.name: Gravitational Search Algorithm
algorithms.time: O(N K D) per iteration plus N objective evaluations, with K decreasing from the population toward the published 2% terminal fraction
algorithms.applicability: Bounded continuous derivative-free optimization using fitness-dependent masses, decaying gravitational attraction and velocity updates
algorithms.publication: Rashedi, Nezamabadi-pour & Saryazdi (2009), GSA: A Gravitational Search Algorithm, Information Sciences 179(13), 2232-2248
algorithms.implementation: Canonical GSA mass normalization, G(t)=G0 exp(-alpha t/T), elitist Kbest force set decreasing toward 2%, randomly weighted gravitational acceleration, velocity and position updates.
algorithms.assumptions: Finite bounded continuous box and finite objective values; population size at least two; equal-fitness generations use equal normalized masses as the continuous limiting tie case; Kbest is clamped to at least one agent for finite populations.
algorithms.convergence: No universal finite-time global convergence guarantee is asserted; gravitational strength decays exponentially and the published elitist Kbest set shrinks to emphasize exploitation.

algorithms.name: Teaching-Learning-Based Optimization
algorithms.time: O(ND) per iteration plus 2N objective evaluations
algorithms.applicability: Bounded continuous derivative-free optimization using teacher-phase mean displacement and learner-to-learner interaction without algorithm-specific tuning parameters
algorithms.publication: Rao, Savsani & Vakharia (2011), Teaching-learning-based optimization: A novel method for constrained mechanical design optimization problems, Computer-Aided Design 43(3), 303-315
algorithms.implementation: Canonical 2011 TLBO teacher phase with randomly selected teaching factor 1 or 2, followed by the published learner phase and greedy replacement after each candidate evaluation.
algorithms.assumptions: Finite bounded continuous box, finite objective values and at least two learners. The teaching factor is generated internally as 1 or 2 with equal probability and is not an algorithm-specific input parameter.
algorithms.convergence: No universal finite-time global convergence guarantee is asserted; teacher and learner candidates are accepted only when they improve the incumbent under the configured objective sense.

algorithms.name: Crow Search Algorithm
algorithms.time: O(ND) per iteration plus N objective evaluations
algorithms.applicability: Bounded continuous derivative-free optimization using personal hiding-place memory, crow following, flight length and awareness-controlled random relocation
algorithms.publication: Askarzadeh (2016), A novel metaheuristic method for solving constrained engineering optimization problems: Crow search algorithm, Computers & Structures 169, 1-12
algorithms.implementation: Canonical CSA with each crow following another crow memory when the target is unaware, random relocation when it is aware, and personal-memory greedy update; paper benchmark controls fl=2 and AP=0.1 are the defaults.
algorithms.assumptions: Finite bounded continuous box, finite objective values and at least two crows. Flight length and awareness probability are fixed per run; random relocation samples uniformly from the bounded search space.
algorithms.convergence: No universal finite-time global convergence guarantee is asserted; awareness probability controls diversification while flight length controls the scale of directed movement toward remembered hiding places.

algorithms.name: Jaya Algorithm
algorithms.time: O(ND) per iteration plus N objective evaluations
algorithms.applicability: Bounded continuous derivative-free population optimization that moves every variable toward the current best and away from the current worst without algorithm-specific control parameters
algorithms.publication: Rao (2016), Jaya: A simple and new optimization algorithm for solving constrained and unconstrained optimization problems, International Journal of Industrial Engineering Computations 7(1), 19-34
algorithms.implementation: Canonical Jaya best/worst update with per-variable r1/r2 draws, the published absolute-value terms and greedy replacement; population size and iteration budget are the only controls.
algorithms.assumptions: Finite bounded continuous box, finite objective values and at least two candidates. The best and worst candidates are frozen while candidate updates for one iteration are generated; boundary repair is component-wise.
algorithms.convergence: No universal finite-time global convergence guarantee is asserted. Jaya has no algorithm-specific tuning coefficients: stochastic movement is defined only by the current best/worst candidates and uniform random factors.

algorithms.name: Imperialist Competitive Algorithm
algorithms.time: O(ND) per iteration plus assimilation/revolution objective evaluations
algorithms.applicability: Bounded continuous derivative-free optimization using countries, empires, assimilation, revolution and imperialistic competition
algorithms.publication: Atashpaz-Gargari and Lucas (2007), Imperialist competitive algorithm: An algorithm for optimization inspired by imperialistic competition, IEEE Congress on Evolutionary Computation, 4661-4667
algorithms.implementation: Canonical ICA lifecycle with fitness-ranked imperialists, probabilistic colony allocation, beta-scaled assimilation with angular deviation, revolution, imperialist/colony exchange and weakest-empire competition.
algorithms.assumptions: Finite bounded continuous box and finite objective values; at least two imperialists and at least one colony. Objective sense is converted only to an order-equivalent competition cost.
algorithms.convergence: No universal finite-time global convergence guarantee is asserted; assimilation, revolution and imperialistic competition preserve the stochastic search mechanism of the 2007 ICA.

algorithms.name: Black Hole Algorithm
algorithms.time: O(ND) per iteration plus N-1 attraction evaluations and event-horizon replacement evaluations
algorithms.applicability: Positive-cost bounded continuous minimization using attraction to the current black hole and event-horizon replacement
algorithms.publication: Hatamlou (2013), Black hole: A new heuristic optimization approach for data clustering, Information Sciences 222, 175-184
algorithms.implementation: Canonical Black Hole Algorithm: every star moves toward the current best using one uniform scalar, a better star becomes the black hole, and stars inside the published event horizon are reinitialized.
